                                                Abstract
     Random geometric graphs are random graph models defined on metric measure spaces. A
     random geometric graph is generated by first sampling points from a metric space and then
     connecting each pair of sampled points independently with a probability that depends on
     their distance.
         In recent work of Huang, Jiradilok, and Mossel Huang et al. (2024), the authors study
     the problem of reconstructing an embedded manifold form a random geometric graph sam-
     pled from the manifold, where edge probabilities depend monotonically on the Euclidean
     distance between the embedded points. They show that, under mild regularity assump-
     tions on the manifold, the sampling measure, and the connection probability function, it
     is possible to recover the pairwise Euclidean distances of the embedded sampled points up
     to a vanishing error as the number of vertices grows.
         In this work we consider a similar and arguably more natural problem where the metric
     is the Riemannian metric on the manifold. Again points are sampled from the manifold
     and a random graph is generated where the connection probability is monotone in the
     Riemannian distance. Perhaps surprisingly we obtain stronger results in this setup. Unlike
     the previous work that only considered dense graph we provide reconstruction algorithms
     from sparse graphs with average degree n1/2 polylog(n), where n denotes the number of
     vertices. Our algorithm is also a more efficient algorithm for distance reconstruction with
     improved error bounds. The local distance-estimation part runs in O(n2 polylog(n)) time,
     and the final all-pairs shortest-path step gives an overall running time of O(n3 ). Our
     distance error also nearly matches the volumetric lower bounds for distance estimation.


1. Introduction
Random graphs provide a powerful framework for modeling complex networks. The clas-
sical Erdős–Rényi model G(n, p), in which edges appear independently with probability p,
remains a cornerstone of modern probabilistic combinatorics, offering analytic clarity for
studying connectivity, typical distances, and phase transitions. Comprehensive references
include Bollobás (2011); Janson et al. (2011) and the survey Frieze and Karoński (2015).
    To model more complex and realistic graphs it is natural to consider edge probabilities
that depend on spatial or geometric proximity. Random geometric graphs (RGGs) model
this phenomenon by associating latent positions to vertices and defining adjacency as a func-
tion of distance. In the classical hard-disc model, two vertices v, w are connected whenever

     An exciting new research direction in the study of RGGs concerns the extent to which
one can infer latent geometric or probabilistic structure from the observed connectivity pat-
tern. Earlier work established detectability thresholds distinguishing geometric graphs from
Erdős–Rényi graphs in various regimes Bubeck et al. (2016); Liu et al. (2022); Brennan et al.
(2020). Other studies have explored nonparametric inference for translation-invariant RGGs
on spheres, aiming to recover the connection kernel p(⟨x, y⟩) from a single graph Araya and
De Castro (2019); Eldan et al. (2022); Duchemin and De Castro (2023).
     A recent work of Huang, Jiradilok, and Mossel Huang et al. (2024) initiated the study of
distance reconstruction from a single random geometric graph sampled on a manifold. Con-
ceptually, this frames a geometric inverse problem: to what extent can the metric structure
of a continuous space be recovered from a single noisy combinatorial observation? They ad-
dressed this problem under a relatively mild set of assumptions: In their model, one observes
a graph generated from i.i.d. samples X1 , . . . , Xn ∼ µ on a smooth, compact, connected d-
dimensional submanifold M ⊂ RN (without boundary), where each edge {i, j} is included
independently with probability p(∥Xi − Xj ∥), with p non-increasing and bi-Lipschitz on
[0, diam(M )], and µ satisfying a lower Ahlfors regularity condition (see Assumption 1.3).
Assuming additionally that p, d, curvature bounds, and a quantitative non-self-intersection
bound are provided, they give an O(n3 )-time algorithm that reconstructs all pairwise am-
bient Euclidean distances (up to vanishing error) with high probability.

1.1. Our Contributions and comparison to prior work.
In this paper, we consider a different natural variant of the question studied in Huang et al.
(2024). Here, we consider the case where the latent space is a compact Riemannian manifold
(M, g) without boundary, equipped with a probability measure µ satisfying lower Ahlfors
regularity as above. Crucially the probabilities of edges are now determined by a connection
probability function p applied to the intrinsic distance between the points on the manifold.
This is arguably a better model, as for example, on Earth it is more natural to measure
distances by the distance needed to travel rather by the Euclidean distance in 3 dimensions.

Relation to manifold learning. The goal of manifold learning is to infer low-dimensional
geometric structure from data sampled on (or near) an unknown manifold, see e.g. Duchemin
and De Castro (2023); Araya and De Castro (2019); Fefferman et al. (2021, 2020b, 2023);
Atamanchuk et al. (2023) among many others. Our setting differs in a key way: we do
not observe the ambient coordinates or pairwise Euclidean distances, and the neighborhood
graph itself is a single unweighted random graph whose edges appear with probabilities
depending on intrinsic distances. Thus, our problem can be viewed as manifold learning
from connectivity alone, where the main goal is explicit reconstruction of intrinsic distances
(and the induced metric-measure structure), rather than producing a low-dimensional em-
bedding. Indeed, by feeding the output of our algorithm into the framework Fefferman
et al. (2020a, 2021), one can construct a Riemannian manifold that is close to the one
from which the data were sampled. Another line of research related to manifold learning
is due to Aizenbud and Sober (2025, 2021), who consider noisy observations in a tubular
neighborhood of a smooth manifold and develop methods that, for a given query point, es-
timate its projection onto the manifold together with the local tangent space, with provable
consistency and rates.

1.3.4. Triangle comparison, a bridge between the local structure of M and
       the flat Euclidean space.
Although the Nash embedding theorem ensures that any Riemannian manifold can be em-
bedded into a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, our setting differs fundamentally from
that of Huang et al. (2024). In their framework, edge probabilities are determined by Eu-
clidean distances in the ambient space, whereas in ours they depend on geodesic distances
within the manifold. Consequently, even after embedding, Euclidean and geodesic distances
may diverge significantly, which necessitates working directly with the intrinsic Riemannian
structure of M .
    We use the exponential map to identify a small metric ball around p with a ball in the
tangent space Tp M , and we write x̂ for the tangent vector at p pointing to x. The precise
definitions of rinj (M ), the tangent representative x̂, the model spaces Mκd , the opposite-side
function ⋎κ (θ; a, b), and the comparison angles ∡±κ (pxy ) are collected in Appendix B.1.
    Consider two nearby points x, y. When M is flat, the geodesic distance is the Euclidean
distance between their tangent representatives. A basic recurring task in the paper is to
estimate how much the geodesic distance |x y| can differ from this Euclidean proxy under
the sectional curvature bound; let us say that there exists κ > 0 such that the sectional
curvature K of M at any 2–plane σ in Tp M for every p ∈ M satisfies

                                      −κ ≤ K(σ) ≤ κ .

(The existence of such a κ is guaranteed when M is compact.) Rather than expanding
the exponential map and tracking higher-order error terms, we use triangle-comparison
techniques. Specifically, we compare the geodesic triangle with its counterpart in a model
space of constant curvature. The Rauch Comparison Theorem and Toponogov’s Triangle
Comparison Theorem (see e.g. Cheeger and Ebin (2008)) translate the curvature bound
into precise inequalities for side lengths and angles, stated formally in Lemma B.4.
    These comparison bounds form a quantitative bridge between the local geometry of M
and that of its tangent plane. They let us compare the two spaces on a genuinely local,
rather than merely infinitesimal, scale. Equipped with these estimates we may treat M as
almost flat in a sufficiently small neighborhood of p, which in turn allows us to use many
arguments from linear algebra.
